name: Well-Traveled Road Effect
description: Familiar routes can feel faster and easier than they really are, leading people to underestimate travel time or effort compared with unfamiliar paths. The popular label is sometimes broadened to familiar tasks too, but the clearest backing found here is specifically about route familiarity and travel-time judgment.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to wayfinding, repeated internal workflows, and product planning: familiar flows can feel cheaper than they objectively are, which can distort ETA promises, migration estimates, and assumptions about how much friction repeat users still face.
myth_risk_note: This pass's search hit a total homonym collision on the metaphorical phrase 'well-traveled road' rather than the travel-time psychological effect. Existing corpus backing (Jafarpour & Spiers 2016) stands unaffected; the entry's own partial status already reflects that broader generalization beyond route-specific contexts lacks direct validation.
prevalence_note: Appears on broad cognitive-bias lists and occasional decision/design-writing posts, but it is not a standard named law in mainstream UX curricula or behavioral-design canon.

findings.description: A PRISMA-based systematic review of 94 studies on route familiarity in transport psychology found that familiar routes reduce cognitive control devoted to processing the environment, increase mind wandering, increase recall accuracy, and decrease perceived task difficulty relative to unfamiliar routes -- establishing route familiarity as a robust, well-studied phenomenon with real cognitive and behavioral consequences, fully independent of the Jafarpour & Spiers lab. Honest scope note: this review's own reported outcomes (attention, cognitive control, task difficulty) are broader route-familiarity effects, not a direct restatement of Jafarpour & Spiers' specific 'subjective travel time contracts' finding -- it substantially broadens the independent evidence base for route-familiarity effects within the travel/transport domain (the domain this entry's partial status already scopes it to) without itself replicating the precise time-contraction metric.
findings.source_title: The role of route familiarity in traffic participants' behaviour and transport psychology research: A systematic review

findings.description: In international students who had lived for 9 months around a London college district, greater route familiarity expanded sketch-map space but contracted estimated travel time: familiar everyday routes were judged as taking less time to traverse than less familiar parts of the same environment.
findings.source_title: Familiarity expands space and contracts time
